subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 12 periods = 480 minutes
Total: 12 periods · 8h 0min

periods.activity_title: Before We Read: Launching into Paper Boats

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.109): pre-reading oral warm-up — paper boats and predictions.

time_bands.activity: Open with the title 'Paper Boats' on the board and invite students to share freely what the words bring to mind — a quick paired exchange before sharing with the class.

Guide students through the two remaining pre-reading prompts from 'Let us read' (p.109): what someone might hope for when they send a paper boat down a stream, and what the poem might be about — elicit a range of predictions.
Read the poem aloud at an unhurried pace, with students following in their textbooks (pp.109–110); pause at each stanza to let the imagery settle before moving to the next.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening brings students into the poem's world of childhood wonder and longing before analysis begins; establishing the wistful, wonder-filled tone early will anchor later work on imagery and symbolism. A common pitfall is rushing the read-aloud — Tagore's poem depends on cumulative imagery (paper boats, shiuli flowers, clouds as sails, midnight stars), so an unhurried reading aloud matters.
materials: Board or chart for recording student predictions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.109): match highlighted words to meanings — running, bulging, lading.
Let us discuss (p.111): choose correct words to complete the poem summary.

time_bands.activity: Return briefly to the poem text (pp.109–110) and ask students to locate the highlighted words — running, bulging, lading — in context before attempting meanings.
Work through the word-matching activity from 'Let us read' (p.109) — students attempt matches in pairs, then share with the class; teacher confirms meanings by pointing back to the poem lines.
Guide students through the fill-in-the-summary task from 'Let us discuss' (p.111); take answers stanza by stanza, asking students to read the relevant poem lines aloud to justify each choice.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem aloud, students now consolidate word meanings and the poem's narrative arc; the summary task is valuable because it asks students to sequence the poem's progression from day to night. Watch for confusion between 'running' (flowing) and 'speedily' — contextual re-reading of the relevant line usually resolves it.

periods.activity_title: Theme, Tone, and Alliteration in the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.111): choose correct option for the poem's themes.
Let us discuss (p.111): identify whether the setting statement is true or false.
Let us discuss (p.111): complete tone and mood blanks from given choices.
Let us discuss (p.111): identify examples of alliteration from the poem.

time_bands.activity: Students work individually on the theme multiple-choice and the true/false setting statement from 'Let us discuss' (p.111); brief whole-class discussion to confirm and reason through each answer.
Take up the tone-and-mood fill-in from 'Let us discuss' (p.111); ask students to read one or two lines aloud that most clearly show the gentle, wishful tone before filling in the blanks.

Students scan the poem for examples of alliteration from 'Let us discuss' (p.111); pairs share finds, teacher lists them on the board and reads each aloud so the sound pattern is heard, not just seen.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through the poem's narrative in the previous task, students are now ready to name its literary and tonal qualities; the alliteration hunt is particularly effective when students read the phrases aloud rather than just underlining them. Students often conflate 'theme' with 'plot' — anchoring each theme option (innocence, imagination, playfulness) to a specific stanza helps clarify the distinction.

periods.activity_title: Imagery, Repetition, and Symbolism in the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.111): fill blanks on repetition and imagery words from the poem.
Let us discuss (p.112): match poem symbols (paper boats, shiuli flowers, midnight stars) to meanings.

time_bands.activity: Students work on the fill-in task about repetition and imagery from 'Let us discuss' (p.111); teacher draws attention to 'day by day' and 'float on and on' as examples before students find additional instances.

Introduce the symbolism matching task from 'Let us discuss' (p.112) — paper boats, shiuli flowers, midnight stars; students attempt matches in pairs, then the class discusses the reasoning behind each match with reference to the poem text.

periods.teacher_notes: The shift from noticing alliteration and imagery to interpreting symbolism marks a move toward critical reading; the symbolism task works best when students justify their matches by re-reading the relevant lines. A common difficulty is distinguishing the literal meaning of 'shiuli flowers' (garden blooms carried on the boats) from their symbolic meaning (purity and transience) — encouraging students to ask 'what feeling does this image create?' helps bridge the gap.

periods.activity_title: Extract Analysis: Night, Fairies, and the Dreaming Child

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.112–113): extract questions on the night stanza — speaker, feelings, fairies.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.113): answer the three reflective questions on personal details and imagination.

time_bands.activity: Read the final stanza aloud together — 'When night comes I bury my face in my arms…' — and ask students what emotion they hear before opening the extract questions.

Work through the extract questions from 'Let us think and reflect' (pp.112–113) one by one: who is the speaker, what the speaker feels at night, what kind of beings the fairies of sleep are, and what 'lading is their baskets full of dreams' suggests — discuss each as a class before students record answers.
Preview the homework questions (p.113) briefly so students know what reflective thinking is expected; teacher models one line of reasoning for the first question without giving the answer away.

periods.teacher_notes: Having mapped the poem's symbolism, students can now work closely with the final stanza's dream-world imagery; the extract questions move from literal identification to gentle inference about the speaker's inner life. Students often find 'lading is their baskets full of dreams' opaque — connecting 'lading' to the cargo/loading meaning established in the word-matching work (p.109) usually unlocks the image.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Sai and Her Father: The World of Origami

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.114): select true statements from the origami conversation.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the listening task context: a girl named Sai and her father are talking about paper-folding; read the seven statements from 'Let us listen' (p.114) aloud so students know what to listen for.
Teacher reads the conversation transcript (p.137) aloud at a natural pace, with students following the seven statements; a second reading is done at a slightly slower pace for those who need it.

Students record their true/false judgements for each statement, then discuss as a class — for each answer, students point to the specific part of the conversation that confirms or contradicts the statement.

periods.teacher_notes: The origami conversation connects naturally to the paper-boat world of the poem, keeping the thematic thread alive while shifting to a new skill; the task tests careful listening for factual detail across a sustained dialogue. A common error is marking statement 4 ('people have been making paper cranes for thousands of years') as true — the transcript says 'hundreds of years' and over 'a thousand years ago' for the origin, not the cranes specifically, so this distinction is worth drawing out.

periods.activity_title: Show and Tell: Presenting an Eco-Friendly Craft

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.115): plan and deliver an eco-friendly craft presentation to the class.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the presentation framework from 'Let us speak' (p.115) — introduction, description, reason for liking it, conclusion — and model a brief example so students understand the expected structure and the phrase prompts.

Students take a quick planning time to decide on their craft item and sketch out their four-part structure using the phrase prompts; teacher circulates and helps students who are unsure what craft to choose.
Selected students deliver their presentations; class listens and offers one appreciative observation each — teacher gives brief spoken feedback focusing on structure and use of the phrase prompts.

periods.teacher_notes: The speaking task grows from the chapter's paper-and-craft world; the four-part structure given in 'Let us speak' (p.115) gives students a scaffold without removing the need to speak in their own words. Students often default to describing only what the craft looks like — encouraging them to explain the process and why the craft matters to them produces richer presentations.
materials: Board listing the four presentation parts and phrase prompts

periods.activity_title: Writing a Diary Entry: Joy of a Rainy Day

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.116): write a complete diary entry about the joy of a rainy day.

time_bands.activity: Discuss the features of a diary entry from 'Let us write' (p.116) — date/time heading, opening feeling sentence, details, concluding remark — and read the given opening sentence together so students absorb the register.

Students draft their diary entries independently, following the guidelines; teacher circulates, offering quiet prompts to students who stall after the opening sentence — suggest sensory details (sound of rain, smell of wet earth, feel of cool air).

Students swap entries with a partner for a brief peer response — one specific detail they found vivid, one suggestion for a stronger concluding remark; then students revise their concluding remark before the period ends.

periods.teacher_notes: The diary form connects the poem's personal, first-person voice to a real-world writing context; the rainy-day prompt allows students to bring in the kind of sensory, joyful observation that runs through 'Paper Boats' itself. Students often lose the personal, reflective tone of a diary and slip into a narrative report — reminding them that a diary is written for themselves, not an audience, usually brings the tone back.

periods.activity_title: Building 'of' Phrases from the Poem's Language

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.113): create 'of' phrases by combining Column 1 and Column 2 words.
Let us learn (p.114): sort time-of-day words into Morning/Afternoon/Evening/Night columns.

time_bands.activity: Revisit 'blooms of the dawn' and 'fairies of sleep' from the poem and ask students what grammatical structure they share — establish the 'noun + of + noun' pattern before opening the task.

Students work through the phrase-building task from 'Let us learn' (p.113), combining Column 1 and Column 2 words with 'of'; pairs compete to create the most phrases before sharing with the class — teacher lists favourites on the board.

Move to the time-of-day sorting task from 'Let us learn' (p.114) — students place words like twilight, forenoon, noonday, nightfall into the four columns; pairs compare choices and resolve any disagreements using the poem's own time words (dawn, night, midnight) as anchors.

periods.teacher_notes: The phrase-building task grows directly from Tagore's own poetic language; connecting the grammar point to lines students have already read and discussed makes the pattern feel natural rather than mechanical. Students tend to confuse 'dusk', 'nightfall' and 'twilight' — pointing out that all three describe the transition between day and night usually prompts a useful class discussion about precision in word choice.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.114): match poem words to their antonyms — strange, dawn, launch, bulging, float, lading.

time_bands.activity: Read each of the six vocabulary words (strange, dawn, launch, bulging, float, lading) in the poem line where they appear; students predict the antonym before seeing Column 2, to activate prior knowledge.

Students complete the antonym matching task from 'Let us learn' (p.114) individually; teacher draws attention to pairs that require understanding the poem's context — particularly 'lading/emptying' and 'bulging/shrinking'.

Class review of matches; for each pair, ask students to compose an original short sentence using the antonym in a context related to the poem's imagery — sharing two or three aloud consolidates the vocabulary.

periods.teacher_notes: Having sorted time-of-day vocabulary, students now work with antonyms drawn directly from the poem's language, reinforcing the contextual meanings they have built across earlier reading. Students often match 'launch' with 'sink' (confusing it with 'float') — returning to the poem line 'I launch my paper boats' and asking what the opposite of launching an object onto water would be clarifies the distinction.
materials: Textbook open to pp.109–110 and p.114

periods.activity_title: Fragrant Flowers and Water Riddles: Exploring Beyond the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.116): research fragrant flowers locally; write names in two languages, draw and colour two.
Let us explore (p.117): solve the four water riddles and share answers with the class.

time_bands.activity: Introduce shiuli (night-jasmine) as the poem's connecting flower and explain that 'Let us explore' (p.116) asks students to think about fragrant flowering plants from their own locality — briefly discuss what 'fragrant' means and name one or two examples together.

Students work on the flower research task from 'Let us explore' (p.116): list at least two fragrant plants from their area with names in their home language and English, then draw and colour two flowers on a blank page — teacher circulates and prompts students to think of plants from their gardens, school compound or neighbourhood.

Read the four water riddles from 'Let us explore' (p.117) aloud one at a time; students work in pairs to solve each before sharing answers with the class — teacher links each answer back to the poem's stream imagery where natural.

periods.teacher_notes: The shiuli flower in the poem becomes a bridge to students' own natural environments; the two-language naming task honours local knowledge while building English vocabulary. Students sometimes struggle to name plants in English — encouraging them to start with the home-language name and then look up or ask for the English equivalent makes the task accessible rather than frustrating.
materials: Blank paper and colouring tools for flower drawings

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: From Paper Boats to Personal Voice

time_bands.activity: Revisit the poem's central journey — from the child writing his name on paper boats to the fairies of sleep sailing them under midnight stars — through a brief whole-class discussion: what did the child want, and did imagination help him reach it?

Students work in pairs to identify one image from the poem that moved from the real (stream, garden, sky) into the fantastical (clouds as sails, fairies of sleep), and explain in two sentences how Tagore made that transition; pairs share with the class.

Students write a short personal reflection (ten to twelve sentences) responding to the poem's core idea: if you could send a message out into the world — like the child's paper boats — what would it say, and why? The writing begins and ends in this sitting; students read their final sentence aloud to a partner before the period closes.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws on the poem's full arc — its imagery, symbolism, tone, literary devices and the day-to-night movement — as well as the chapter's broader work on craft, listening and personal expression; students bring all of that to bear on a fresh, open reflective task. The writing prompt is deliberately personal so it cannot be answered without having inhabited the poem's world; watch for responses that summarise the poem rather than respond to its invitation — a quiet reminder that the question asks 'what would your message say?' usually redirects students.

items.source_lo: Student reads and responds to a poem using literary-reading and critical-reading strategies as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Tagore's poem: paper boats, shiuli flowers, clouds as sails, fairies of sleep, day-to-night arc, symbolism, alliteration, tone.
items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 110 beginning "I load my little boats with shiuli flower". Which of the following best describes why the child-speaker loads shiuli flowers onto the paper boats?

options.label: A
options.text: To attract the fairies of sleep to come and sail the boats at night.

options.label: B
options.text: To carry the freshness of dawn out into the night and the unknown world.

options.label: C
options.text: To decorate the boats so that the sky-playmate can recognise them.

options.label: D
options.text: To make the boats heavier so they float more steadily on the stream.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Students who choose this are reading the image literally — a load is physical weight — rather than as a symbolic gesture of hope.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Students who choose this conflate two separate stanzas; the fairies appear only in the night-dream stanza, not in connection with the flowers.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Students who choose this conflate the clouds-as-sky-playmate stanza with the flower-loading stanza, merging two distinct imaginative acts.

items.source_lo: Student reads and responds to a poem using literary-reading and critical-reading strategies as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Tagore's poem: paper boats, shiuli flowers, clouds as sails, fairies of sleep, day-to-night arc, symbolism, alliteration, tone.
items.item_stem: In 'Paper Boats', the child-speaker writes his name and village on the boats, loads them with shiuli flowers, watches clouds become sails, and dreams of fairies sailing the boats under midnight stars. How does Tagore use the contrast between day and night to show that the child's imagination works as a bridge between the real world and the unknown? Support your answer with at least two specific images from the poem.

expected_elements: Identifies a daytime image grounded in the real: stream, garden, sky.
Identifies a night-time image that is fantastical: fairies, midnight stars, dreams.
Explains how the contrast shows imagination bridging self and unknown world.
Uses specific poem language or imagery to support the argument.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a spoken conversation and identifies factually accurate information using listen-and-respond strategies as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Sai and her father's dialogue about origami history, paper cranes, the thousand-cranes belief, and creative process.
items.item_stem: Listen to the conversation between Sai and her father about origami. Then read the statements below and write TRUE or FALSE for each. Give one word or phrase from the conversation to support each TRUE answer.

options.text: According to a belief in Japanese culture, folding a thousand paper cranes allows you to make a wish.
Origami began in Japan more than a thousand years ago.
Paper cranes became popular for decorative fun from the very beginning of origami.
Sai's father practised origami when he was a child.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the father says 'I remember doing that when I was your age.'
2. True — the father says 'Origami started in Japan over a thousand years ago.'
3. False — the transcript states it was not until the seventeenth century that people began making animals and flowers just for fun; originally paper was reserved for special occasions.
4. True — the father says 'there is a belief that if you fold a thousand paper cranes, you can make a wish, and it will come true.'

items.source_lo: Student listens to a spoken conversation and identifies factually accurate information using listen-and-respond strategies as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Sai and her father's dialogue about origami history, paper cranes, the thousand-cranes belief, and creative process.
items.item_stem: In the conversation, Sai's father says that origami is not just about the final shape. What does he say it is really about? In your own words, explain what you think he means, and give one example from the conversation that shows this idea in action.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Sai's father says origami is about the process, the patience and the creativity involved. He shows this when he offers to sit with Sai and help her finish the crane together, valuing the making over the end product.

items.item_stem: Think of a simple object you could make at home using eco-friendly or recycled materials — for example, a paper windmill, a leaf bookmark, or a seed-packet envelope. Describe your chosen object to a partner: what it is, what it is made of, and one thing that makes it special to you. Use complete sentences and speak clearly.

expected_elements: Names the object clearly and states the material it is made from.
Describes the object's appearance — colour, shape, or size.
Explains one way the object is personally meaningful or useful.
Speaks in complete sentences at an audible, steady pace.

items.item_stem: The child in 'Paper Boats' sends paper boats downstream hoping someone far away will find them and know who he is. Imagine you are presenting your eco-friendly craft to an audience from another school who have never met you. Give a short two-minute presentation that introduces both your craft and yourself — explain what inspired you to make it and why you would want someone in a different place to have it.

expected_elements: Introduces themselves and the craft with a clear opening sentence.
States what inspired the choice — a personal reason or connection.
Explains why someone from another place might value or enjoy the craft.
Closes with a sentence that connects the craft to the idea of reaching out to others.

items.source_context: Diary entry guidelines: date/time heading, personal opening, sensory details, concluding remark; rainy-day joy prompt.
items.item_stem: Write a diary entry about a day when you noticed something in nature that made you feel happy or wonder-struck — it could be a sudden shower, a flower blooming, a bird's call, or the night sky. Use the correct diary format: include a date and time heading, begin with how you were feeling, give two or three specific sensory details, and end with a personal remark.

expected_elements: Correct diary format: date, time heading, and 'Dear Diary' opening.
Personal, first-person voice throughout — not a narrative report.
At least two specific sensory details (sight, sound, smell, touch, or taste).
A concluding personal remark that reflects on the feeling, not just the event.

items.source_lo: Student writes a personal diary entry in the appropriate form and register using guided-writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Diary entry guidelines: date/time heading, personal opening, sensory details, concluding remark; rainy-day joy prompt.
items.item_stem: In 'Paper Boats', the child-speaker uses his imagination to turn a simple act — floating paper boats — into a message sent out to the whole world. Write a diary entry from the child-speaker's point of view, on the evening after floating the boats. In your entry, describe what the child saw, felt and hoped for, and end with what the child wishes might happen by morning.

expected_elements: Written in first person as the child-speaker, with diary format observed.
Includes specific detail from the poem: stream, name-writing, shiuli flowers, or clouds.
Expresses the child's longing to be known by someone in a 'strange land'.
Ending wish is imaginative and connects to the poem's night-and-dream imagery.

items.item_stem: Tagore uses the noun-of-noun pattern to create images like 'blooms of the dawn' and 'fairies of sleep'. Choose any TWO of the following word pairs and use each to build your own 'noun of noun' phrase. Then write one sentence for each phrase that shows its meaning clearly. Word pairs: (wings, evening) — (tears, rain) — (shadows, night) — (songs, wind).

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Responses will vary; a strong answer builds a grammatically correct 'noun of noun' phrase from the given pair (e.g., 'wings of the evening') and writes a sentence that makes the meaning of the phrase clear and imaginative (e.g., 'The wings of the evening spread quietly across the sky as the last light faded').

items.source_lo: Student extends the poem's themes through local inquiry and wordplay using hands-on exploration as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Shiuli flowers and local fragrant plants named in two languages; four riddles about bodies of water connected to the poem's stream.
items.item_stem: The child in 'Paper Boats' launches his boats on a running stream. Think of a body of water you know from your own experience — a river, a pond, a lake, or the sea. Write a short riddle (four to six lines) about it, the way the 'Let us explore' riddles are written. Your riddle should use at least one image from the natural world (an animal, a plant, or a time of day) without naming the body of water directly.

expected_elements: Describes the body of water using sensory or natural images, not its name.
Includes at least one image from the natural world — animal, plant, or time of day.
Uses a riddling structure: clues build toward a single answer.
Shows a connection to the poem's world — water, movement, or the natural environment.

items.source_lo: Student extends the poem's themes through local inquiry and wordplay using hands-on exploration as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Shiuli flowers and local fragrant plants named in two languages; four riddles about bodies of water connected to the poem's stream.
items.item_stem: Shiuli flowers appear in 'Paper Boats' as a symbol of purity and the freshness of dawn. Choose one fragrant flower or plant from your locality. Find out: (a) its name in your home language and in English, (b) the time of year it blooms, and (c) any story, belief or use connected to it in your community. Present your findings as a short illustrated fact-file: a drawing of the flower, its two names, its blooming season, and two to three sentences about its significance.

expected_elements: Provides the flower's name in both the home language and English.
States the blooming season accurately based on local knowledge.
Gives a brief community story, belief or practical use connected to the flower.
Includes a drawing that is recognisably of the chosen flower.
